compounding_issues: Seed's tasks table lacked owner_id, forcing session 2 to bolt on a runtime ALTER TABLE migration that still runs inside init_db every boot through session 5
Seed shipped insecure auth (static-salt SHA256 + opaque DB token store), so session 2 had to do a full security rewrite instead of incremental feature work — early technical debt absorbed mid-story
Session 3's Celery notification is coupled at import time (app.py imports send_notification_email and calls .delay directly), so the app needs celery/redis at load; only tests' mocker keeps it green
Session 5 rate limiting hard-depends on Redis storage (flask_limiter storage_uri), adding external infrastructure to what was otherwise a self-contained sqlite-only app
Per-request connections via `with get_db()` commit but never close — a latent resource-leak pattern carried unchanged from the seed through all 5 sessions
Session 5 (cross-cutting) became the largest session at ~80K tokens, concentrating rate limiting + pagination + tests into one expensive overloaded commit
key_decisions: Session 1: build the tasks domain (table + CRUD blueprint + tests) on top of the auth seed, initially reusing the seed's DB-backed token scheme
Session 2: replace static-salt hashing and DB tokens with werkzeug password hashing + real JWT (PyJWT HS256) and scope all task routes behind @require_auth with owner_id
Session 3: introduce Celery for async email notifications on task completion, routed to a dedicated 'email' queue via celery_config
Session 4: extract a repository layer (BaseRepository + User/Task/Items repositories), removing inline SQL from route handlers
Session 5: add user-keyed rate limiting (flask_limiter keyed on JWT sub) and cursor-based pagination on list_tasks, both built on the session 2 auth and session 4 repository foundations
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. The story opens on a security-weak seed (static-salt hashing, opaque DB tokens, owner-less tasks) and session 1 is conservative, adding the task_manager domain while inheriting the seed's auth flaws. Session 2 delivers the sharpest jump: a full auth hardening (real JWT, werkzeug hashing) plus owner-scoped tasks with a migration, converting the early_degrade seed's weaknesses into strengths. Session 3 adds a reasonable async-notification integration, session 4 is a clean, behavior-preserving repository refactor, and session 5 lands operational features (rate limiting, pagination) that build directly on the earlier auth and repository layers. Test coverage grew monotonically from 16 to 46 tests, all passing at every commit, ending at a ~0.98 test:code ratio across 520 code lines with 93.7% cache hit rate and zero cascade recovery, showing consistent, compounding engineering rather than decay.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc that starts from a degraded seed, hardens and repays early security debt in session 2, then compounds through integration, refactor, and cross-cutting features with monotonically growing, all-green test coverage.
